value.overview: The Peruvian Booby (Sula variegata) is a highly social seabird of the cool, nutrient-rich Humboldt Current along the Pacific coast of South America. It is strongly associated with anchovy-rich marine waters and breeds in large colonies on coastal islands and cliffs. Most of its population occurs from northern Peru to central Chile, with occasional northward movements or vagrancy reaching farther along the Pacific coast, including rare records in Costa Rica.
value.classification: The Peruvian Booby belongs to the family Sulidae, which includes boobies and gannets, and the genus Sula. It is a monotypic species without currently recognized subspecies.
value.identification: This is a large, long-winged booby with a white head, neck, breast, and belly, contrasting with dark brown to black upperparts and wing margins. Adults have a grayish bill, dark facial skin, and gray feet. The plumage often shows white spotting or scaling on the dark wing coverts. In flight, it appears sleek and strongly contrasting black and white. It can resemble Blue-footed or other dark-backed boobies, but its gray feet and mostly coastal South American distribution are useful clues.
value.rangeHabitat: The main range follows the Pacific coast from southwestern Ecuador and northern Peru southward through Chile to the Chiloé region. It uses cold, productive coastal waters, usually close to shore, where it plunge-dives for schooling fish. Breeding colonies are located on offshore islands, rocky shores, cliffs, and sloping guano-covered terrain. In Costa Rica it is not a regular resident or breeder; it is a very rare visitor or vagrant, chiefly associated with the Pacific coast and offshore waters. Records should be carefully documented because the species is uncommon there.
value.migrationStatus: Generally sedentary or dispersive rather than a long-distance migrant. Individuals may move widely in response to changes in prey availability, especially during El Niño conditions. In Costa Rica it occurs only exceptionally as a rare Pacific-coast or offshore vagrant, with no established seasonal population known.
value.breeding: Peruvian Boobies breed colonially, often in dense aggregations on bare islands, rocky slopes, and cliff ledges. Nesting material commonly includes guano, small stones, vegetation, and other debris. Both adults share incubation and chick-rearing duties. Usually several eggs may be laid, although clutch size and breeding success vary with food availability. Incubation lasts about six weeks, and young remain dependent in the nest for several months before fledging. Breeding is concentrated in Peru and Chile, not Costa Rica.
value.dietFeeding: The diet consists mainly of small schooling marine fish, especially Peruvian anchoveta, with sardines and other pelagic fish also taken. The species forages by flying over the sea and diving steeply into the water, often entering at high speed. It commonly feeds in groups where prey schools are concentrated and may forage within a few kilometers of breeding colonies, although birds can travel farther when food is scarce.
value.behavior: This is a strongly gregarious seabird that rests, travels, and feeds in groups. Birds often fly low over the sea in lines or loose formations and gather in large colonies during breeding. Territorial displays at nest sites include head movements, pointing postures, threats, and bill jabbing. Peruvian Boobies are powerful fliers and capable divers. Their movements and breeding success are closely linked to ocean conditions and the availability of anchovy and other schooling fish.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population trend is not clearly established. Numbers may vary markedly between years because food supply, ocean temperature, and breeding conditions affect colony attendance and reproductive success.
